attacker.model: claude (Kiro subagent; exact model version not exposed to the agent)

notApplicable.null-vs-empty: The only input is an int; no text input exists. A NULL value is already a fixed case (REPLICATE with a NULL length is NULL).
notApplicable.collation-case: No text input; the result is never compared as text.
notApplicable.trailing-spaces: No text input; CONVERT(varchar(8), int) never adds spaces.
notApplicable.numeric-rounding: The input is an int; no decimal or money value.
notApplicable.top-ties: Scalar function: returns one value, no rows from tables.
notApplicable.identity-gaps: Reads no table, no key or sequence.

cases.label: -1 keeps its sign inside the padding: '000000-1'
cases.reasoning: T-SQL pads the string '-1' with REPLICATE('0', 8 - DATALENGTH) on the left, so the zeros go before the sign. A to_char or lpad of abs() with a leading sign would give '-0000001'.

cases.label: -1000000 (exactly 8 characters with the sign) is unchanged
cases.reasoning: 8 characters including the sign fits varchar(8) exactly: REPLICATE('0', 0) is ''. A length test that counts digits only (not the sign) would treat it as 7 and pad, or as too long.

cases.label: -99999999 (9 characters with the sign) does not fit varchar(8): '0000000*'
cases.reasoning: 8 digits but 9 characters with the sign. A check on the number of digits (or on abs(value) > 99999999) would keep it and lpad would truncate; SQL Server's CONVERT gives '*'.

cases.label: 10000000 (8 digits, smallest 8-digit value) is unchanged
cases.reasoning: Lower boundary of the 8-character range from below; an off-by-one in the length test (>= 8 instead of > 8) would turn it into '*'.

cases.label: 9999999 (7 digits) gets one leading zero: '09999999'
cases.reasoning: One below the 8-digit boundary; REPLICATE('0', 1). An integer-division or log10-based length would be off by one here.

cases.label: -10 keeps its sign inside the padding: '00000-10'
cases.reasoning: Two-digit negative value; checks that the sign counts as one character of the 8 (DATALENGTH of varchar counts bytes, one per ASCII character).

cases.label: 2147483646 (one below int maximum) gives '0000000*'
cases.reasoning: Large positive value next to the int maximum; an implementation that adds 1 or works in a narrower type would overflow or truncate instead of returning '*'.

cases.label: -2147483647 (one above int minimum) gives '0000000*'
cases.reasoning: Large negative value next to the int minimum, where abs() is still representable; a digit-count test via abs() would give a different branch than at the minimum itself.
